documents.text: The Banking Code of Practice is the Australian banking industry's code, published by the Australian Banking Association (ABA). The 2025 Banking Code of Practice was approved by ASIC on 27 June 2024 and is effective from 28 February 2025. The independent Banking Code Compliance Committee monitors banks' compliance with the Code. The Code replaces the version dated 5 October 2021. A 2026 Banking Code Review is underway.

documents.title: Banking Code: help for customers in financial difficulty
documents.source: Australian Banking Association – Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025)
documents.keywords: financial difficulty hardship Banking Code hardship interest only extend loan defer payments superannuation debt sold financial counsellor What does the Banking Code say about hardship? Can my bank make me use my super to pay my loan? Can the bank sell my debt while I'm in hardship?
questions: What does the Banking Code say about hardship?
Can my bank make me use my super to pay my loan?
Can the bank sell my debt while I'm in hardship?
documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), Financial Difficulty means being unable to repay what you owe, expecting to be unable to pay upcoming repayments, or having difficulty meeting repayment obligations. Examples of help include short-term interest-only payments, extending the loan term to reduce repayments, or temporarily postponing or deferring payments, which may increase total interest. The bank will tell the customer in writing whether it will help and the reasons for its decision. Customers can ask the bank to deal with their financial counsellor or representative. The bank will not require a customer to access superannuation to repay a loan (unless borrowing for a self-managed super fund), and will not sell the debt while actively considering the customer's financial situation.

documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), before accepting a guarantee the bank will take reasonable steps to hold a meeting with the prospective guarantor, in person or by video, phone or other means, without the borrower present, unless the guarantor has received independent legal advice or another exception applies. The bank will not accept a guarantee until the third day after the guarantor has been given the required information, unless an exception applies. Within 14 days of the relevant event, the bank will send the guarantor copies of formal demands or default notices, and notices about borrower hardship changes or a continuing default of more than two months.

documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), banks will take reasonable measures to make their services accessible, including for older customers, people with disability, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander customers and people with limited English. Where practicable, banks will organise or refer customers to free external support, including interpreter services (including Auslan) and the National Relay Service. Banks will help Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander customers meet identification requirements when they lack standard ID documents, following AUSTRAC's guidance. Customers who tell the bank they hold a Commonwealth Seniors Health Card, Health Care Card or Pensioner Concession Card will be given information about basic, low-fee or no-fee accounts.

documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), banks commit to taking extra care with customers who are experiencing vulnerability. Circumstances the Code lists include age, disability, mental health conditions, elder abuse, family and/or domestic violence, financial abuse, Financial Difficulty and language barriers. The Code encourages customers to tell their bank about their circumstances so the bank can provide appropriate support.

documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), once a bank has received the verified documents it needs, it will act on a valid Deceased Estate Representative instruction about a deceased's accounts within 14 business days. For accounts in the deceased's sole name, the bank will promptly identify and stop charging fees for banking services that can no longer be provided. Before probate, a representative can still request account information and give instructions to release funds to pay or reimburse permissible expenses such as funeral expenses.

documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), a business is a Small Business if it, together with any related entities, had an annual turnover of less than $10 million in the previous financial year, has fewer than 100 full-time equivalent employees, and has less than $5 million total debt to all credit providers. Small Business customers receive the Code's protections alongside individual customers.

What does the Banking Code Compliance Committee do?
Can the BCCC sort out my complaint against the bank?
documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), a customer who has a complaint, or thinks the bank has not met its obligations under the Code, should contact the bank first, which will try to resolve it through its internal dispute resolution service. If not satisfied, the customer can complain to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) if the complaint fits AFCA's rules; AFCA decisions are binding on the bank, and both routes are free. Customers may also be able to bring a court action. The independent Banking Code Compliance Committee (BCCC) monitors compliance, and suspected breaches can be reported at bankingcode.org.au, but the BCCC is not a complaints resolution body and has no role in addressing and remediating individual complaints.

documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), a customer can ask the bank to cancel a Direct Debit request and the bank will promptly process it. This does not apply to cancelling Recurring Payments made with a debit or credit card, which must be done by contacting the merchant or service provider directly. The customer can ask the bank to investigate an unauthorised Direct Debit, and the bank will act promptly to help. On request, the bank will give a list of Direct Debits and Recurring Payments on the customer's accounts for up to the previous 13 months, limited to those known from its transaction information. Banks will publish information on how Direct Debits or Recurring Payments may be cancelled.

documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), if a customer tells the bank they dispute a card transaction within the time limit set by the credit or debit Card Scheme rules, the bank will claim the amount back if it finds the customer was incorrectly charged and did not contribute to the loss, and may accept the merchant's refusal of the chargeback only if the refusal is allowed under the Card Scheme rules. These rights apply even if the payment was part of a recurring payment arrangement with that merchant. Customers may also have rights to dispute an unauthorised transaction under the ePayments Code or their terms and conditions.

documents.text: Under the Banking Code of Practice (effective 28 February 2025), a guarantee is limited to a specific amount or category of amounts, such as all amounts owing under a specific loan plus items like interest and recovery costs, or to the value of specified property or assets under a mortgage or other security. A guarantor may withdraw by written notice at any time before the bank provides credit under the loan, or afterwards if the signed loan differs in a material respect from the proposed loan given to the guarantor before signing. A guarantor may end their liability by paying the lower of the borrower's outstanding liability or the guarantee limit, or by other arrangements the bank agrees to. If the bank agrees to increase the guarantee limit, it will obtain the guarantor's written acceptance.

documents.title: Financial Claims Scheme: government protection for bank deposits up to $250,000
documents.source: APRA – About the Financial Claims Scheme
documents.keywords: is my money safe bank fails bank collapse government guarantee deposit guarantee 250000 Financial Claims Scheme APRA credit union foreign bank Is my money safe if my bank collapses? Does the government guarantee bank deposits? Who runs the deposit guarantee scheme?
questions: Is my money safe if my bank collapses?

documents.text: The Financial Claims Scheme (FCS) is an Australian Government scheme that protects deposits in authorised deposit-taking institutions (ADIs), such as banks, building societies and credit unions, up to $250,000 per account holder per ADI. APRA, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, says the FCS covers ADIs incorporated in Australia and authorised by APRA. The FCS can be activated by the Australian Government in the unlikely event that an ADI fails, and APRA administers it once activated.

documents.text: APRA says the Financial Claims Scheme limit of $250,000 applies to all of a person's deposits held with one authorised deposit-taking institution (ADI), even when that ADI operates several brands under one banking licence. APRA's examples: St George is part of Westpac, and deposit accounts offered by RAMS are actually Westpac accounts. A person's deposits across these brands are added together and protected up to one $250,000 limit.

documents.text: APRA says a person can have up to $250,000 in deposit accounts with a number of different authorised deposit-taking institutions (ADIs), and each is protected separately under the Financial Claims Scheme. For joint accounts, the amount of Financial Claims Scheme protection is worked out by splitting the deposit equally between the account holders; each account holder's share is then added to any other eligible deposits they hold under their own name at the same ADI.

documents.text: APRA says the Financial Claims Scheme covers savings accounts, call accounts, term deposits, cheque and transaction accounts, cash management accounts, trustee accounts, and mortgage offset accounts (100 per cent or partial offset) that are separate deposit accounts. It does not cover accounts with funds not in Australian dollars, accounts kept at overseas branches of Australian banks, credit balances on credit cards or other loans, or prepaid card facilities and similar products.

documents.source: APRA – FAQs about activation, payments and administration of the Financial Claims Scheme

documents.text: If the Financial Claims Scheme is activated, APRA says it will endeavour to make payments to the majority of account holders within seven calendar days. APRA and the failed institution will tell depositors any steps they need to take to access their payment. Payments are only made in Australian dollars and, in most cases, by cheque or electronically to an alternate account nominated by the account holder. An account holder can make a claim in the institution's liquidation to recover an amount over the $250,000 FCS limit; such claims rank third in priority.

documents.text: The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) says Australian privacy law gives you a general right to access your personal information, except where the law allows an organisation to refuse your request. The OAIC considers 30 days a reasonable period to respond to an access request. An organisation may charge for giving access, but the charge can't be excessive and can't be used to discourage you from requesting access. If it refuses access, it must tell the person in writing its reasons for refusing and how they can make a complaint.

documents.text: The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) says Australian privacy law gives people the right to have personal information corrected if it is inaccurate, out of date, incomplete, irrelevant or misleading, and there is no charge for correction. The OAIC considers 30 days a reasonable time to respond. If an organisation refuses to correct the information, the person can ask it to attach a statement saying the information is wrong, and the organisation must take reasonable steps to do so.

documents.text: The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) says a person must first complain to the organisation they think mishandled their personal information. If the organisation does not respond within 30 days, or the person is unhappy with the response, they can complain to the OAIC; the Privacy Act 1988 requires the complaint to the OAIC to be in writing. For a privacy complaint about a bank, the OAIC says you should contact the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), which has the power to deal with your privacy complaint.

documents.text: Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, explained by the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC), an organisation covered by the Privacy Act has to tell affected people, and the OAIC, if a data breach is likely to cause them serious harm. Generally, an organisation or agency has 30 days to assess whether a data breach is likely to result in serious harm. A notification includes the organisation's contact details, the kinds of information involved, a description of the breach, and recommended steps people can take. Examples of serious harm include identity theft, which can affect finances and credit reports, and financial loss through fraud.

documents.text: The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) says a credit reporting body must give a person access to their consumer credit report for free once every 3 months. A free copy is also available if the person has been refused credit within the past 90 days, or if their credit information has been corrected. The OAIC lists Equifax (138 332) and Experian (1300 783 684) as credit reporting bodies, and notes that credit reporting bodies may hold different information about a person.

An agreed correction must be made within 30 days, or a longer period the person agrees to. If the correction request is refused, the person must be told in writing and told they can access an external dispute resolution scheme or make a complaint.

documents.text: The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) says a person who believes they are, or are likely to be, a victim of fraud, including identity theft, can ask a credit reporting body for a ban period. The ban period lasts 21 days after the request and is free. There is no limit on the number of times a ban period can be extended. During a ban, the credit reporting body generally cannot use or disclose the person's credit report without their written consent.

documents.text: Moneysmart, the Australian Government's financial guidance service run by ASIC, says that when a borrower asks for help, the lender must consider them for hardship assistance. Borrowers can contact the lender's hardship team by phone, email or chat, and Moneysmart says the earlier you seek help, the more options you will have. Hardship help can be temporary, such as deferring a payment, or permanent, such as varying the loan. Moneysmart says a lender must give reasons if it refuses a request for hardship assistance, and the borrower can then complain.

documents.text: Under section 72 of the National Credit Code, a borrower can give their credit provider a hardship notice, verbally or in writing, saying they cannot meet their obligations. ASIC's INFO 105 (updated May 2025) says that if the lender has enough information it must tell the borrower its decision within 21 days, starting the day after it receives the notice. If it needs more information it must ask within 21 days; it then has 21 days from receiving the information to respond, or 28 days from its request if the information is not provided. If the lender does not agree to change the contract, it must give its reasons and the contact details of the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA).

documents.text: ASIC Regulatory Guide 271 sets enforceable internal dispute resolution (IDR) standards for banks and other financial firms, for complaints received from 5 October 2021. ASIC expects firms to acknowledge a complaint within 24 hours (or one business day), or as soon as practicable. A bank must give its IDR response no later than 30 calendar days after receiving a standard complaint. For credit complaints involving default notices, the maximum is 21 calendar days; complaints about hardship notices or requests to postpone enforcement also start at 21 calendar days but have exceptions. If a bank cannot meet the deadline because the complaint is particularly complex or circumstances are beyond its control, it must send an IDR delay notification before the deadline giving the reasons, the right to go to AFCA, and AFCA's contact details.

documents.text: Under ASIC Regulatory Guide 271, a credit provider must give its IDR response to a complaint involving a hardship notice or a request to postpone enforcement proceedings no later than 21 calendar days after receiving the complaint. Exceptions apply. If the credit provider does not have sufficient information to decide, it must request the information no later than 21 calendar days after receiving the complaint, and the complainant must provide it within 21 calendar days. The credit provider then has a further 21 calendar days after receiving the information to respond, or 7 calendar days if the information is not received within 21 calendar days of the request. If agreement is reached, the credit provider has 30 calendar days to confirm the terms in writing.

documents.text: The ePayments Code is a code of practice administered by ASIC, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. ASIC describes it as presently a voluntary code, and most banks, credit unions and building societies subscribe to it. The ePayments Code covers electronic payments such as ATM, EFTPOS and credit card transactions, online and mobile banking, and BPAY. The current version has applied since 2 June 2022. It sets rules on who pays for unauthorised transactions and how mistaken internet payments are handled.

documents.text: Under the ePayments Code (effective 2 June 2022), an account holder is not liable for an unauthorised transaction where it is clear the user did not contribute to the loss, or where the loss was caused by fraud or negligence of bank staff or merchants, forged, faulty, expired or cancelled cards or passcodes, transactions before the card or passcode was received, duplicate debits, or transactions after loss or theft was reported. The bank must prove on the balance of probability that the user contributed through fraud or a passcode security breach, and a breach alone is not enough. Where a passcode was required and no other rule applies, liability is limited to the least of $150 (or lower), the available balance, or the actual loss when reported.

An account holder is not liable for losses from unauthorised transactions that happen after the user has reported the loss, theft or misuse of the card or device, or the breach of passcode security.

documents.text: Under the ePayments Code (effective 2 June 2022), a mistaken internet payment should be reported to your own bank, and the process depends on when it is reported. If reported within 10 business days, and the banks are satisfied a mistaken internet payment has occurred and there are sufficient funds in the recipient's account, the receiving bank must return the funds within 5 business days of the request if practicable, or up to a maximum of 10 business days; if the receiving bank is not satisfied, it may seek the recipient's consent. Between 10 business days and 7 months, the receiving bank investigates within 10 business days and, if satisfied a mistake occurred, freezes the funds for 10 further business days and returns them unless the recipient establishes they are entitled to them. After 7 months, funds are returned only if the unintended recipient consents.

A person is considered to have missed a payment if they make it more than 14 days after the due date. Repayment history appears as a number from 0 to 7 showing the age, in months, of the oldest missed payment, and remains on the credit report for 2 years. Financial hardship information recorded against repayment history remains for one year. The OAIC says a credit provider isn't required to send a written notice before listing a missed payment.

documents.text: The OAIC says a credit provider can list a default only if the payment has been overdue for at least 60 days, the overdue amount is $150 or more, a notice was sent to the person's last known address, a second notice was sent at least 30 days later, and the credit provider waits at least 14 days after the second notice. It can't wait more than 3 months after the second notice to list it. While a hardship request is being decided, and until 14 days after the person is told it is refused, a default can't be listed, unless the request was made on the same basis as one in the previous 4 months. Paying after listing doesn't remove the default, but it is updated to show payment.

documents.text: Westpac lists seven ways a trusted person can help with banking: an authorised third party, an account signatory, account sharing, third-party access, a general power of attorney, an enduring power of attorney, and a financial management order. A general or enduring power of attorney is a legal document, and Westpac's set-up is an in-branch process with legal paperwork and an appointment required; Westpac suggests considering independent legal advice first. A general power of attorney ends if the person can no longer make decisions. An enduring power of attorney must be set up while the person still has capacity to make decisions, and continues after they lose capacity. A financial management order is made by a court or tribunal, usually when the person can no longer make decisions and has no enduring power of attorney.

documents.text: Westpac customers can see all active consents, and past consents that expired or were revoked or cancelled, in the data sharing dashboard in Westpac Online Banking. documents.text: Under the Westpac Online Banking Security Guarantee, if a Westpac account is compromised as a result of internet fraud, Westpac guarantees to repay any missing funds, provided the customer complies with Westpac's Online Banking Terms and Conditions. documents.text: Under Westpac's Debit Mastercard Terms and Conditions (effective 27 August 2026), the account holder is not liable for unauthorised transactions where it is clear the user has not contributed to the loss, including transactions after Westpac was told the card was lost, stolen or misused. The account holder can be liable where the user engaged in fraud, voluntarily disclosed a code to anyone (including a family member or friend), wrote the PIN on the card, acted with extreme carelessness in protecting codes, or unreasonably delayed reporting.
